## Chi-square tests for larger contingency tables

The chi-square test is not limited to $2\times2$ tables.

Suppose we are comparing responses to four treatments, with three possible outcomes:

| | Improved | No change | Worse | Total |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Treatment A | 32 | 13 | 5 | 50 |
| Treatment B | 29 | 13 | 8 | 50 |
| Treatment C | 27 | 11 | 12 | 50 |
| Treatment D | 20 | 15 | 15 | 50 |
| **Total** | **108** | **52** | **40** | **200** |

> **Is response associated with treatment group?**

We can create the contingency table in **R**:

```{webr-r}
tab_treatment <- matrix(
  c(
    32, 13, 5,
    29, 13, 8,
    27, 11, 12,
    20, 15, 15
  ),
  nrow = 4,
  byrow = TRUE
)

rownames(tab_treatment) <- paste("Treatment", LETTERS[1:4])
colnames(tab_treatment) <- c("Improved", "No change", "Worse")

tab_treatment
```

### Compare the observed outcome distributions

As before, we are interested in the outcome proportions **within each group**:

```{webr-r}
prop.table(tab_treatment, margin = 1)
```

The outcome distributions are not the same in our sample.

For example, the proportion who improved ranges from

$$
\large
\frac{32}{50}=0.64
$$

in Treatment A to

$$
\large
\frac{20}{50}=0.40
$$

in Treatment D.

The question is whether the differences among the observed distributions are larger than we would expect from sampling variability if **treatment and response were not associated**.

### Visualize the observed distributions

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

dd <- data.table(
  treatment = rep(
    paste("Treatment", LETTERS[1:4]),
    each = 3
  ),
  response = rep(
    c("Improved", "No change", "Worse"),
    times = 4
  ),
  count = c(
    32, 13, 5,
    29, 13, 8,
    27, 11, 12,
    20, 15, 15
  )
)

ggplot(
  dd,
  aes(
    x = treatment,
    y = count,
    fill = response
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = "fill",
    linewidth = 0.4,
    alpha = 0.95
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Response",
    title = "Observed response distributions"
  )
```

### Expected counts under no association

The overall response proportions are

$$
\large
\frac{108}{200}=0.54,\qquad
\frac{52}{200}=0.26,\qquad
\frac{40}{200}=0.20.
$$

If treatment and response were not associated, we would expect these same proportions in each treatment group.

For example, the expected number of participants who improve in Treatment A is

$$
\large
E_{\text{A, Improved}}
=
\frac{(50)(108)}{200}
=
22.
$$

As before, the expected count for any cell is

$$
\large
E_{ij}
=
\frac{
(\text{row total})(\text{column total})
}{
\text{grand total}
}.
$$

We can obtain all of the expected counts in **R**:

```{webr-r}
chisq.test(tab_treatment)$expected
```

Because each treatment group contains 50 participants, the expected counts are the same for every row:

| | Improved | No change | Worse |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Treatment A | 27 | 13 | 10 |
| Treatment B | 27 | 13 | 10 |
| Treatment C | 27 | 13 | 10 |
| Treatment D | 27 | 13 | 10 |

> Under no association, the response distribution is the same in all four treatment groups.

### Comparing observed and expected counts

Nothing changes about the chi-square statistic:

$$
\large
\chi^2
=
\sum_{i,j}
\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}.
$$

We now simply add the contributions from all **12 cells** in the table.

**R** can do this calculation directly:

```{webr-r}
chi_result <- chisq.test(tab_treatment)

chi_result$statistic
```

### What changes?

The degrees of freedom depend on the dimensions of the contingency table:

$$
\large
df=(r-1)(c-1).
$$

For this $4\times3$ table,

$$
\large
df=(4-1)(3-1)=6.
$$
Here is the $\chi^2_{\text{df=}6}$ denisty with the observed chi-square statistic. The area of the
shaded region is the p-value, which is reported below.

```{webr-r}
#| classes: webr-plot

density_chisq <- data.table(x = seq(0.001, 15, length.out = 1000))

density_chisq[, density := dchisq(x, df = 6)]
# density_chisq <- density_chisq[density <= 0.3]

ggplot(density_chisq, aes(x = x, y = density)) +
  geom_area(
    data = density_chisq[x >= chi_result$statistic],
    fill = "grey60",
    alpha = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(
    x = chi_result$statistic,
    xend = chi_result$statistic,
    y = 0,
    yend = dchisq(chi_result$statistic, df = 6),
    linewidth = 0.2,
    color = "pink"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = expression(chi^2),
    y = "Density",
    title = "Chi-square distribution with df = 6"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.3),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  )
```

Here is the formal test comparing the observed chi-square statistic with a **chi-square distribution with 6 degrees of freedom**.

```{webr-r}
chi_result
```

> **The same idea applies to any $r\times c$ contingency table:** compare the observed counts with the counts expected under no association, and use the chi-square statistic to quantify the discrepancy.
